records.name: Alberta
records.summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.

records.name: Saskatchewan
records.summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

freshness.fact: Policy remains in force: 2025 SKCA 74 allowed the government appeal in part; courts lack jurisdiction to void it while the notwithstanding clause stands

records.name: New Brunswick
records.summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

records.name: Scotland
records.summary:
This region's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category: the region's 2021 hate-crime statute created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the prosecuting authority reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26 (up 21% on 86 the year before), while police recorded 8,538 hate crimes in the provision's first full year. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.

The region's parliament also passed a more expansive self-declaration gender-recognition law with a two-thirds majority in December 2022 - evidence of markedly more trans-accepting regional institutions - only for the central government to block it with the first-ever use of a statutory veto order; verification as of September 2026 confirms the bill fell and remains not law, with no revival. The same UK-wide rules on legal sex and single-sex services apply here as across the union state.

records.name: Distrito Federal
records.summary:
CDMX recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the city's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide made a distinct crime in July 2024 ("Ley Paola Buenrostro", the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created December 2024 covering all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requiring feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines (72h/48h); a new Gender Police launched August 2025 with 30 patrol units. Long-standing LGR since 2014, extended to 12-year-olds by 2021 decree. For a visitor assaulted in CDMX, there is trained machinery to investigate; in Nuevo León (0.40) or Michoacán (0.40) there is none.

Modestly above the national 0.55: the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.

freshness.fact: CDMX remains Mexico's most protective jurisdiction: gender-ID change since 2008, conversion-therapy ban 2020, non-binary registration added 2025; the 2024 transfeminicide aggravated-offence reform stands.

records.name: Nuevo Leon
records.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force

records.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
records.summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026), who also located most attacks on the community in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence. Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026 — a suspect was arrested, a positive institutional response. Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026, one of them a gay man, were linked by the attorney general's office to organised crime. An NGO observatory report counted 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024, led by Morelia (11), then Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5) and Zamora (4), with 2015 the deadliest year (10 victims).

Colectivo PRIDE Michoacán reports rising attacks in the municipalities bordering Jalisco, that victims are no longer attended to, and that the state does not acknowledge the violence. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol — the only counterweights are individual arrests.

Context for comparison: Veracruz, similarly hostile, at least passed a gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025; Mexico City pairs comparable lethality with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocols. Michoacán has no legal machinery whatsoever, plus an armed-group amplifier that makes the violence harder to escape or report.

records.who: MEX/Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
records.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
records.summary:
Veracruz led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6), with 19 of 32 states recording victims that year. In 2025 the state closed the year with at least 15 hate crimes against the LGBT+ community; a January 2025 running total put 460 hate-crime cases unresolved, and Emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences. Activists cite 'rezago y archivamiento de expedientes' (deliberate filing-away of cases), and the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely; in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the family reported that the homicide file had simply disappeared, and organisers call the 2025 pride march a platform against that impunity. The killing of 'Luis M', a 27-year-old trans woman stabbed to death in a motel in Oluta on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted 9 hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women; the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as Veracruz's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

The only institutional counterweight is recent: Veracruz passed its gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025 with no age limit, among the last to legislate one (2025): 22 of 32 states had a procedure by March 2025.
